stops.name: Jinja, Ripon Falls, down the Nile
stops.campa: Striking camp after the turn of the year, the party crosses into Uganda and comes to Jinja, where the Nile pours out of Lake Victoria over the Ripon Falls and begins its four-thousand-mile argument with the desert. They embark northward with a paddle-steamer and a narrow-gauge patience, through Sudd and heat, Jung feverless and watchful, riding the river that runs like time itself from the lake-heart of Africa toward the tombs. He has chosen to leave Africa by the oldest road in the world, stern first, facing the interior.

stops.name: Aswan, Egypt entered from the south
stops.campa: By Khartoum and the desert rail the travelers descend into Egypt not as tourists from the Mediterranean but from within, from the south, from the source: the direction of the Nile itself and of the black Hamitic root under the pharaonic tree. At Aswan the granite islands stand in the brown water; northward wait the temples, where Jung reads the Horus-cry to the rising sun as the elder brother of the Elgonyi's spittle-offering. Africa closes behind him like a book whose sentence he was: the light is completed by the one who beholds it.

stops.name: Küsnacht, the Golden Flower arrives from Wilhelm
stops.campa: Jung paints a mandala with a golden castle at its centre and is troubled by its Chinese air: the forms, the colors, nothing European in it. As the paint dries, the post brings a package from Richard Wilhelm in Frankfurt: the manuscript of a thousand-year-old Taoist alchemical treatise, The Secret of the Golden Flower, with the request that he write a commentary. The coincidence breaks the isolation of a decade: his inner geometry has correspondents across the world and back through the centuries. He writes the word for it under the painting, and the word is synchronicity; and the road into alchemy stands open.
stops.quote: In remembrance of this coincidence, this 'synchronicity,' I wrote underneath the picture: 'In 1928, when I was painting this picture, showing the golden, well-fortified castle, Richard Wilhelm in Frankfurt sent me the thousand-year-old Chinese text on the yellow castle, the germ of the immortal body.'

stops.name: Zurich, Psychology Club, the Kundalini seminar
stops.campa: In the Psychology Club at Gemeindestrasse 27, following the indologist Wilhelm Hauer's exposition, Jung delivers his psychological commentary on Kundalini yoga: the chakras read as a ladder of consciousness, the serpent-fire as the perilous ascent of the impersonal within the personal. He warns the room like a mountain guide: these are not exercises for Europeans to imitate but a map by which to recognize where the psyche's weather is already carrying them. The East is admitted to the consulting room, on Swiss terms, with ropes.

stops.name: Berlin, the seminar in the darkening Reich
stops.campa: In the first summer of the new Reich Jung gives a week's seminar in Berlin on dreams, before an audience in which enthusiasm and dread sit in the same chairs. He has seen this weather before (in 1918 he wrote of the blond beast stirring in its underground prison), and he watches Wotan, the old wind-god of his mother's people, take possession of a nation as he once took a single dreaming woman. The years that follow will tangle his name in the storm; the register records the seminar, the warning, and the wind.

stops.name: Eranos, Ascona-Moscia, the round table below Monte Verità
stops.campa: On the terraced shore of Lake Maggiore at Moscia, below Monte Verità, the corpus's own hill of anarchists, dancers and sun-worshippers, Olga Fröbe-Kapteyn opens the first Eranos Tagung, the shared meal of the spirit, and Jung lectures on the process of individuation. Under the cedars, at the round table by the water, the learning of Europe and Asia sits down together each August: Corbin will bring the angel of Persia, Scholem the Kabbalah, Zimmer the gods of India, Kerényi the Greeks. For nearly two decades this garden is the capital of Jung's public thought: a Goethean colony on the Goethe atlas, facing south.

stops.name: Bombay, India entered
stops.campa: Invited by the British-Indian government to the jubilee of the Indian Science Congress, Jung lands at Bombay in December and India rises around him: a dreamlike world of temple crowds, ochre saints, and a civilization that never expelled the opposites. He resolves to travel it as he traveled Africa: not to convert or be converted, but to see Europe again from a great distance. He declines, throughout, to call on the holy men, wishing to owe his truth to no guru: a discourtesy he commits deliberately, and confesses in the canon.

stops.name: Sanchi, the hill of the stupas
stops.campa: At Sanchi, on the green hill where the great stupa has stood since Ashoka, an unexpected emotion seizes Jung with the force of possession: the stillness of the domes, the gates carved with the whole breathing world, the distant plain. Here Buddhism becomes real to him at a stroke: the Buddha understood as the self that outgrows the gods, the wheel set turning by a man. He walks the circumambulation path clockwise with the pilgrims, a Basel doctor pacing the oldest circle he has yet joined, and the hill accepts him.

stops.name: Konarak, the black pagoda
stops.campa: At Konarak on the Orissa shore Jung walks around the Black Pagoda, the fallen sun-temple built as the chariot of Surya, its wheels taller than men, its walls a surf of gods coupling in stone. His pandit explains, whispering, that the obscene sculptures are a means to spiritualization: the common man must be reminded of his dharma as flesh before he can be led beyond it. Jung, whose first dream was a phallus enthroned underground, receives the lecture with the composure of a man being shown his own childhood by strangers. The sun-wheel and the man-eater are one temple here, above ground, unashamed.

stops.name: Calcutta, the fever
stops.campa: At Calcutta, garlanded with the honorary doctorates of Allahabad, Benares and Calcutta (Islam, Hinduism and British-Indian medicine in three hoods), Jung is felled by dysentery and lies ten days in the English hospital. The fever is India's last argument: the subcontinent, he says later, was becoming too much, and the illness a device to remove him from the flood of impressions into a white room. In the enforced stillness the psyche prepares its verdict on the whole journey, and delivers it as only it delivers anything: as a dream.

stops.name: Calcutta, the dream of the Grail refused to the subcontinent
stops.campa: Convalescent in the hospital, Jung dreams himself with his friends on an unknown island off the south coast of England, where in a dark castle the celebration of the Grail is to be held tonight, but the Grail is not yet there, and he must swim the cold channel alone to fetch it. Imperiously the dream wipes India from him: not for him the wisdom of the yogis; his task lies with the neglected Grail of the West, the unhealed Christian vessel. He rises homeward bound and never leaves the ship at the ports of return, reading Grail texts in his cabin the whole way.
stops.quote: Imperiously, the dream wiped away all the intense impressions of India and swept me back to the too-long-neglected concerns of the Occident, which had formerly been expressed in the quest for the Holy Grail.

stops.name: Kandy, the drums of the Tooth, and home
stops.campa: In the hill temple at Kandy, before the relic of the Buddha's tooth, Jung hears the evening drummers in the mandapam play the drum-language of sacrifice: young men drumming to the young Buddha as the Elgonyi breathed to the young sun. Ceylon he receives as the antechamber of paradise and the end of the eastern road. Then the ship, the cabin, the Grail books; India astern like a great dream one honours by not imitating. He carries home the black pagoda, the stupa hill, and the refusal: the freight of a man sent back to finish his own religion.
